Since this fragment is of rare and pleasing subject matter, and since neither Father Busaeus, who gathered Trithemius’s spiritual works into one volume, nor before him Marquard Freher, Palatine Councillor, who comprised Trithemius’s historical works in two tomes, added it to their volumes, it has pleased me, learned reader, to set it here before you to be read and discussed, so that I might both rescue it from destruction and at the same time give you the pleasure of an agreeable reading.

Farewell, and enjoy it.

On the Reprobate and Witches

The fifth question.

Question Five

The fifth question of your most serene Highness was this: Why can impious, evil, and reprobate people in matters of faith, such as those women whom we commonly call witches, command malignant spirits, when good men and the most zealous observers of the Christian faith can command neither good spirits nor always malignant ones?

I remember that I formerly answered this question as follows. In all the works of the divine majesty, the sequence and order of beauty belong to an inviolable equity, by which each thing, fittingly disposed, persists in the rank it has received. For, without its proper order, the freedom of will that the Creator of all gave to human beings is driven by no violence of power so as not always to remain in the order that the first human being received from the beginning of his creation. Therefore no one among mortals is good unless, assisted by the counsel of his own will, he is made so through the grace of the merciful God; and no one is evil unless, by his own choice, he is deprived of grace because of the obstacle of sin.

By uprightness of will, however, we are made like the good spirits, if we prove the piety of the faith that we have in Christ by holy and necessary works. And just as the perfection of a good will makes good men equal to angelic spirits, so the perversity of the impious makes them like demons. Hence, the more evil and perverse people have been corrupted by the malice of their own will, the more they become like demons in disposition. But likeness introduces the familiarity of friendship, and from this there gradually arises the confidence of the lesser toward the greater, and command, whether it is real or feigned by trickery. Thus, if there seems to be any command of wicked people over demons, it arises from the magnitude of their depravity, namely when their disposition is so corrupted that, by a reprobate will, they either surpass or equal the malice of the demons associating with them.

For not all demons are equal in malice or intelligence, but one is much craftier than another in swiftness of understanding, and far worse in corrupted affection. For those who, having fallen from the lofty seats, are more closely joined to the earth and inhabit caverns and caves are certainly duller than the rest, even to such a degree that they fear swords and rods and seem to be moved by the threats of people who terrify them, as one may observe in those whom we call demoniacs. But demons who dwell farther removed from the earth are of a subtler nature and more rarely meet with human beings. Yet the more people full of malice advance in perversity of will, the more like demons they become; and once admitted by them into familiarity, they thereafter become bold and receive command over the demons whose familiarity they use, not by violent power but by feigned simulation.

For demons, in order to keep those people whom they have once received into their submission willing participants in their depravity, gladly subject themselves to them as though moved by a simulated domination; and what they do of their own accord, they pretend to do as if compelled to obedience. For no one obtains true command over demons except the person whom faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, through the merit of holiness, has made acceptable and a friend to God. For thus Scripture says concerning those who truly believe in the Lord Jesus: “And he gave them power over all demons.” Therefore evil people command demons because malevolence has made them like them, likeness has made them familiar with them, and familiarity has made them their own and subject to them. Just as, if some servant born in a humble station, joined by daily familiarity to a great prince, as often happens, is said to command him from whom he has everything he obtains, without contradiction, everything he has asked for, so that he himself seems rather to rule his lord than to be ruled by him. In accordance with this comparison, wicked and reprobate people are admitted by demons into their familiarity, and through a more prolonged confidence they become very bold. They receive a simulated, not a true familiar, command over them, which they have merited by the likeness of a most depraved will. Hence whatever they request from demons who cooperate with them by an implicit or explicit pact, they receive, except when, being prevented by divine ordinance, the demons are unable to provide what is asked. Yet they do not cooperate in this way indiscriminately with all the reprobate and wicked, but only with those with whom, by the intervention of some pact, they have entered into covenants, such as sorcerous women, who have paid homage to the devil, and those invokers of demons whom the common people call by the usual term necromancers.

There are two kinds of people who can lawfully command demons. The first is that of those people who, beloved by God through the merit of holiness, have received from him the power to trample on the head of the ancient serpent. Such were the apostles in the primitive Church, and their followers and disciples, of whom the Lord says in the holy Gospel: In my name they will cast out demons, and they will take up serpents. The second kind is that of those people to whom, by reason of their order in the Church of God, it is granted to drive demons from human bodies by the received power of their ministry. And this ministry is entrusted to exorcists in the Church of God, when, that is, they are ordained by the bishop.

Again, there are two kinds of people who desire to command demons, and the most wicked conditions show how unlawfully they presume to do this. The first and most destructive kind is that of sorceresses, who enter into pacts with demons and, after a solemn profession has been made, hand themselves over to some demon as a perpetual right of property and obedience. How great are the evils this most destructive kind of people commits in your empire, most wise Caesar, there is no one who can express it. For first denying God, the faith of Christ, and holy baptism, they offer themselves in mind and body to demons; by their sorceries they sicken, injure, and kill human beings and beasts. There is no disease that, with God permitting it, they cannot bring on, because when they present themselves to demons as servants in observance of the pact they have made, in comparison with them they dare whatever they wish. Hence they are not to be tolerated anywhere, but rather to be utterly exterminated in every place, as God the Creator of all commands: You shall not suffer sorcerers to live.

Some sorceresses call demons by spells, others entice them by prayers and sacrifices, and the rest, provoking them with unspeakable things and ceremonies, draw them into the aid of their impiety. Therefore it is no wonder that a sorceress seems to command demons, since through the piety of a perverse will they have been made like them, and by mutual association they are united for the evil of the human race. The second kind of depraved people who wish to command demons is that of those whom people commonly call necromancers. They profess arts full of curses, by which they promise that they can summon demons into a circle, or show them plainly visible when enclosed in crystal or some other vessel. These most destructive people, full of falsehood and superstitions, commit evils so great that no good person could imagine them. For in order to entice demons into their service, they very often use most shameful sacrifices and enter into an explicit pact with them. They carry around many various little books full of filth, impiety, and falsehood, and falsely inscribed with the names of ancient philosophers and sages; by displaying these they deceive many unwary and curious people and drag them with themselves into the pit of demons. They promise great and utterly incredible things, and by the hearing of these they deceptively hold people in wonder. With rings, pentacles, images, exorcisms, and conjurations, they say Questionum: They say that they can constrain malignant demons, so that they appear visibly in a circle, or in a crystal, or in some other receptacle, and answer distinctly to all questions asked. All of them indeed promise this, but in our times very few are found whom the malignant spirits obey in this way, even among the wicked, since God, for a most just reason, does not permit it, lest human curiosity, prone to novelties, should despise the religion of Christ and in time of need seek help from demons. But all those whom malignant spirits, summoned by the conjurations of necromancers, obey, have without doubt passed into their fellowship through an explicit or implicit pact. Yet the greater number are the others, whom the malignant spirits disdain to obey, although they are never afraid at any time to busy themselves in the profane arts of necromancers. And because in our own times especially iniquity has begun to abound, and the charity of many has grown cold, these accursed and most deceitful men have gained too much strength; and although they are despised by demons, nevertheless, persisting in their pernicious doctrines, they deceive many. Believe me, Caesar: this most deceitful race of men is very harmful to your sacred empire, and therefore must be utterly exterminated no less than the source of witches. They promise great things, and they lie about everything. For indeed all the things promised in their books are empty and false, and they give believers nothing other than tricks, frauds, and most subtle deceptions. But if at any time they seem to display what they have promised, it is manifest to everyone that this happens only through the cooperation of demons, from whose fellowship one must flee no less than from the most savage torments of hell. For demons very often come to these necromantic operations, and, in order to keep their invokers stubborn in the treachery they have begun, grant them what they ask if they can. Sometimes, however, when invoked by conjurations, they disdain to appear, and nevertheless they have led astray the minds of those invoking them.

Questionum. 83 There is also another class of people, no less foolish than superstitious: namely, those who do not wish to have any commerce with demons, and nevertheless use, in empty operations, things appropriated to demons, and for that reason wholly unlawful. For they think that great and hidden power inheres in characters, and therefore they commit various errors against the faith of Christ. But because this is not the time to recount their madness, let us pursue our purpose. Why good and just people do not obtain command over demons must be stated briefly.

Just as likeness of wills makes wicked and impious people equal to demons, so unlikeness of wills renders the good and just wholly opposed to them. Between opposites and dissimilar things there can be no familiarity; rather, continual resistance and hatred prevail. But where no familiarity contracted through likeness of wills is found, neither confidence

[Marginal note:] Magical characters are demonic according to Trithemius. [Marginal note:] The good are hated by demons, not familiar with them.

can exist from one toward another, nor any mutual cooperation in the working of marvels. Nor do you, glorious Caesar, since you are a man, the great governor and prince of men, admit anyone into familiarity with you who is wholly opposed and unlike you in morals, and who continually resists your will. But because good and upright men always oppose the most depraved will of demons, they can in no way pass into fellowship with those with whom they neither wish nor consent to be familiar; rather, they flee and detest their encounter with all their strength. And therefore they do not obtain that fictive command over them of which we have spoken. For nowhere is familiarity secure when no likeness of wills has preceded it; nor can there be concord between opposites, nor friendship stand firm between those of unlike will. Yet demons do not obey all evil and reprobate people indiscriminately, but only those with whom they are bound by pacts and acts of service; and when invoked they willingly come to those whom they cannot otherwise have as faithful servants, although though they falsely claim that they are being compelled. It is therefore no wonder, most excellent Caesar, that malignant spirits sometimes seem to obey depraved and perverse human beings, whom, as we have said, malevolence has made like themselves and destructiveness toward the human race has made to be in agreement with them. But let it be far from every Christian to wish to command demons through a wicked likeness of will, since if anyone in this life has begun to have fellowship with malignant spirits, in the life to come he will burn with them without end.

But why are good and just people unable to command the holy angels of God, into whose likeness they have passed by good will? I think that, from what has been said above, the solution of this question would easily be given, if the difference of intellects were recalled to mind. For although there are many people established in the Church of God whose justice helps many toward salvation, nevertheless in our times very few advance so far that, by the merit of holiness, they are either feared by demons or received into the fellowship of familiarity by angels. Hence it comes about that people of our time neither command malignant spirits by the merit of holiness, nor deserve to be familiar with the holy angels. But if any have advanced to that degree of holiness in which, performing miracles in the Church, they have advanced as the saints once did, then they can both command demons powerfully and have the familiar fellowship of blessed spirits. For it is certain that holy people beloved by God in the primitive Church of Christians once bestowed greater benefits on mortals through the working of good spirits than the impiety of depraved people could ever have inflicted as harms by the ministry of demons. For whoever is a true worshiper of God, if he has become like the holy angels, can do many wondrous things by prayers.

On the Power of Witches

Question Six

The sixth question of your most invincible Majesty was: whence comes this so great power in witches, who can accomplish so many, varied, and wondrous things even in a single hour, things such and so great that none of the good could accomplish them in his whole life?

If we wish to answer this question briefly, we must necessarily say that all power is from the Lord God, without whom no creature can do anything. For Christ says in the holy Gospel: Without me you can do nothing. Hence it is manifest that all power of doing anything is granted to human beings by the Lord God, and from nowhere else, whether people do good or do evil. Thus the most holy bishop Augustine says: The will of God is the first and highest cause of all bodily forms and motions, and nothing comes to be in this most extensive and immense commonwealth of the whole creation, visibly, unless it is either commanded or permitted from the inner, invisible, and intelligible court of the supreme Emperor, according to the ineffable justice of rewards and punishments. Hence there is no doubt, Caesar, that that power of little witches, by which they produce wondrous and horrendous effects with the cooperation of demons, is granted by the Lord God, whose will no one can resist, and without whose influence a human being cannot even move his hand. For the holy doctors conclude that neither demons nor witches can do anything, whether to harm a human being or a beast of burden, unless almighty God wills, consents, and grants the power that they may do what they have already determined by a perverse will. Unless God consents and wills, no creature can do anything. Otherwise, if something could happen when he did not will and consent to it, it would necessarily follow that God was utterly weak, since he could not prohibit what, against his will, he would be forced to permit. But since every human being, man, insofar as he is a creature, depends on God and can do nothing without the will of him from whom he has both the will and the power. Therefore whatever witches do is done by God's permission; without his will they can do nothing, because, unless God grants that they can do what they wish, they will obtain it neither from themselves nor from demons. Thus every power is from the Lord God, in whom all things exist and are moved, as in the first cause of all things, since from him from whom we have received freedom of choice we also have the ability to do what we will.

But since the understanding of witches is very confused, they perpetrate the evils they do not by human art, but by the cooperation of demons. Nature has made demons subtle, and long experience has made them swift in producing marvels. For the wondrous effects of witches are not caused by such means as they use for witchcraft, such as heads of the dead, toads, serpents, characters, images, and things of this sort, but by the devil who instituted these signs; since he is most proud, he desires to seem comparable to God in all things. Indeed, just as almighty God has instituted certain sacraments in his Church, which, when worthily administered and with his assistance, signify and produce a saving effect, he who instituted them bringing about salvation, so also the devil, who desires nothing more than to be regarded as equal to God, has instituted certain signs as if they were sacraments. When he is invoked by those with whom the malignant worker has been allied by pacts, he is present; and whenever God permits it, he effects the evil that is asked. If God does not permit it, he does absolutely nothing.

For the devil is the agent of all necromantic effects and of witches' effects; through the application of the means which he himself previously instituted, he produces the desired work in the matter subjected to him, sometimes in reality, sometimes only in appearance. But witches, women who have already been transferred by depraved will and by consent into the fellowship of demons through pacts, receive from them certain marks and symbolic signs, by which, once summoned, the demons immediately appear. In these pernicious operations of the demon nothing is stronger than the foolish credulity of witches, which is increased by pacts and vows; for the firmer the faith they have placed either in demons or in their signs, the more swiftly they attain the operation through their cooperation.

For the exceedingly savage depravity of witches' will in a certain way turns them into frenzy; when this has taken possession of the mind, the demons immediately attach themselves to the raging women and, invited by pacts and signs, with God's permission, furnish to the madwomen the effect of their request. Plato related something similar in the book On Poetic Frenzy, saying: Just as Bacchant women, when not of sound mind, draw honey and milk from rivers, but when of sound mind cannot draw them. This is brought about by their spirit, carried outside itself into fellowship with an evil demon. We have it as an established fact that witches have drawn butter from stirred-up rivers at times, something that can in no way happen otherwise than by the ministry of a demon. In the same way, when they have been turned to hatred against some person or beast of burden, and are breathing out its destruction, they are driven by a most grievous frenzy, thinking of nothing in their mind except revenge. They have recourse to witchcrafts known and familiar to them, invoke demons, display the signs instituted by them, and at the same time the characters; and what they cannot accomplish by their own power, they obtain through the demons' ministry.

But another person, who is not subject to demons by pact and surrender, even if he knows the things suitable for witchcraft and also the manner of working, and although he displays the signs, nevertheless rarely obtains the effect, because he is not counted among the demons' familiars. For the devil, swollen with pride, imitates the Church of Christ to such a degree that, just as one who is not ordained cannot consecrate the body of Christ, however much he may pronounce the words of consecration, so also the demon, however much someone invokes him and displays signs or characters, either never or rarely comes to the aid of one whom he does not know to be subject to him by pact. For if he made himself available everywhere to all who invoked him without pacts if he came indiscriminately to all who invoked him, without pacts being set between them, he would not possess so many witches dedicated to him by right of ownership. Hence it is that many who are devoted to profane arts labor to summon demons to a circle, to a mirror, or to any other receptacles by dreadful conjurations, and obtain no effect: because either God’s command stands in the way, or the devil despises the curious person who has not been devoted to him by homage.

For three things are required for witchcraft, without which it is clear that none is perpetrated: a witch raging in spirit and of depraved will, the cooperation of a familiar devil, and, before all else, divine permission. For if one of these does not concur, she will not be able to perpetrate witchcraft. For if God did not permit it, neither the devil nor the witch could do anything. And if the devil did not meet the will of the wicked woman, she would perpetrate no witchcraft. Again, if the witch were lacking, the devil would by no means bring witchcraft to completion. For the devil uses the will of the raging witch as a craftsman uses an instrument for working, without which he could not inflict witchcraft.

And just as demons differ from one another in power and in sharpness of subtlety, so the power of witches is not one and the same in all, but differs in individuals according as they are joined by demons of subtler or grosser nature. For there are many kinds of demons, and they stand apart from one another in fixed ranks by reason of the places into which, when they fell at the beginning, they were thrust down.

The first kind of demons is called fiery. It roams about the higher air, and is never plunged down to lower regions before the day of judgment; rather, remaining continually beneath the lunar regions, they have no intercourse with human beings on earth. That they remain beneath the moon is attested by Saint Augustine in the work On the Christian Combat, saying thus: Demons do not dwell in the heaven where the sun and stars are, but all move about beneath the lunar region. Moved by this, as I think, Apuleius said that demons are fiery animals, because Aristotle affirmed that in burning furnaces certain small animals have rather often been seen flying about, fitted with little wings, which pass their whole life in fire, since they arise with fire and are extinguished with it, and, vanishing, return to their own place whence they had come. They have no association with witches, since, because they dwell in fire, on account of their subtlety they cannot put on a gross or aerial body.

The second kind is called aerial, which wanders in the air and dwells near us. These indeed can descend to the lower regions and, having assumed bodies from the denser air, sometimes appear visibly to human beings. With God permitting, they quite often disturb the air, stir up thunder and storms, and all together conspire for the destruction of the human race. After the manner of human beings they are moved by the affections of passions, especially pride and envy, and are touched by continual disturbances; and they are neither clothed in a customary body, nor do they remain in one place. Nor do they all have one form, but many, and these they change rather often according to the variety of the affections by which they are either summoned by witches’ charms or driven by disturbance to do harm. For they have an altogether violent and furious disposition, full of agitation; hence, when they have been greatly injured and disturbed, they contrive sudden ambushes for the most part, and while they carry out their attacks, they partly wish to remain hidden and partly inflict violence.

Witches supported by the cooperation of these demons are the more powerful for practicing witchcraft, the higher the order of the demon they have obtained as their associate. In the Life of Saint Antony, the blessed Athanasius said that the air is full of demons, which Mercury, called Thrice-Greatest, had said before: namely, that no part of the world is without the presence of demons. The holy bishop Ambrose also says: The world is full of holy powers, because it is full of wickednesses. Hence the Platonists have reported that demons flying in the air, in the manner of very dense fiery snow, are visible to those who desire it.

visible, if for some time, while the sun is shining, they continue to gaze toward the sky with unflinching eyes. But I do not know whether the object is produced in the air from a real substance, or whether rather the checked motion of the eyes presents false images; nevertheless I have made trial of what was promised, not without some slight harm to the sense of sight.

We call the third kind of demons terrestrial, whom we do not at all doubt to have fallen from heaven to earth according to their deserts. Concerning these, the most holy bishop and martyr of Christ, Theophorus, once Ignatius, wrote thus in a certain letter to the Ephesians: Nothing is better than to have peace, in which every weapon of the aerial and terrestrial spirits alike is made void. Of these demons, some dwell in woods and groves and set snares for hunters; others live in open fields and make travelers wander astray at night; some remain in hidden places and caves; the rest, less furious and disturbed than the others, take delight in dwelling with human beings in obscurity.

They are not led by one passion, but by various ones, since some are less depraved than others, although all are full of evil disturbances. Of these, some delight in frightening human beings only with illusions; others wish, by predictions of future things, to draw their hearers into admiration of themselves. Some, however, labor with the greatest effort to terrify, injure, or kill human beings who are disturbed by irrational fury or raging with melancholy; we have learned by experience that this has often happened. Hence Saint John Chrysostom says in the third book On Providence, to the monk Stagirius: More powerful for doing harm than every diabolical action is the greatness of sorrow, because whomever the demon overcomes, he overcomes through sorrow. If you remove it, no one will be able to be harmed by a demon.

This kind of demon is rarely familiar to witches, because of the inconstancy of their passions and the levity by which they delight in frightening many people rather than being subject to the command of one little woman. Yet at times, as they promise to the insane, they dwell in glass, crystal, or a mirror, and, stirred up by charms, they give answers to women; and if anyone who is coming has spoken ill of them, they announce it beforehand on the road.

And this kind of witch sometimes differs greatly from the rest, since what the others make infirm by sorcery, these women promise to cure. But because for the most part they repel sorcery by sorcery, access to them is forbidden by the Church to every Christian.

The fourth kind of demons is called aquatic, since, immersing itself in waters, it dwells around lakes and rivers. It is full of anger, disturbed, restless, and deceitful; it stirs up storms at sea and, sinking ships into the deep, takes life from many in the waters. And whenever these demons assume a visible body, they more often appear in the female sex, and are seen more rarely in the male, because they frequent moist places and follow a softer course of life, nor can they easily assume a common form by the habit of the others.

Hence antiquity long ago named the Naiads and Nereids, nymphs of the waters, not in the masculine sex but in the feminine. Among our people, moreover, they are called by the common term aquatic women, that is, Wasserfrauen. But those who live in drier and somewhat arid places, whenever they appear bodily to human beings, transform themselves visibly into men. They also assume the forms of various beasts, according as they are touched by various passions. Holy angels, however, since they never vary in passion, always appear uniformly in male form. For we nowhere read it written that a good spirit was seen in the form of a woman or of any beast, but always in male appearance. Yet demons have very often been seen around rivers and springs in the appearance of women, sometimes dancing in choruses, sometimes loosening their hair in the manner of women, and at times speaking with human beings and practicing various deceptions. And this kind of demon is not accustomed to have dealings with acts of sorcery.

The fifth kind is called subterranean, because it dwells in caves and caverns and in the remote hollows of mountains. These demons are of the worst disposition, and they especially attack those who dig wells and mines, and those who seek treasures hidden in the earth, being most ready for the destruction of the human race. They make openings in the earth, stir up flame-spewing winds, and shake the foundations of buildings. Sometimes at night they go out from the mountains in bands and lead strange and astonishing dances in the fields; and, as if fearing the command of a single leader, they suddenly vanish at a sign and return to their own hiding places. At times the sound of bells is heard among them, and they sometimes falsely claim that they are the spirits of people who have died. They seek nothing more than human fear and amazement. Hence we have found that they have sometimes led some of the simpler sort of people into their hiding places in the mountains, showing astonishing spectacles to those who marvel at them, and, as if there were dwellings of the blessed there, they falsely pretend to be friends of the living. Among these demons, too, some are guardians of treasures, which the avarice of mortals has hidden in the earth; and, lest they should again come into human use, they withdraw them, steal them, guard them, and sometimes move them from place to place. This kind of demon is not accustomed to have any commerce with women’s acts of witchcraft.

The sixth kind of demons is called light-fleeing, because they greatly abhor and detest the light: for they never appear by day, nor can they assume a body in any way except at night. This is the business that walks about in darkness, an inscrutable and utterly dark kind of demon, stirred by cold passions, malicious, restless, and disturbed, which violently oppresses people it meets during the hours of night, and quite often, with God’s permission, kills them either by a certain breath or by touch. This kind of demon does not associate with acts of witchcraft, nor can it be constrained by charms, because it flees both light and human voices, and likewise every tumult. The aerial kind is especially accustomed to attend the witchcraft of women, since it is subtler than all the others and of the boldest rashness. Some of the terrestrial demons also, as has been said, serve certain acts of witchcraft; yet, being of a lower rank, they cannot at all bring about those greater acts of witchcraft. It is therefore manifestly clear that the whole power of acts of witchcraft, in which they do such astonishing things, is granted to demons in limited measure by the Lord God; and when he does not permit it, they accomplish nothing.

On Divine Permission

Question Seven

The seventh question of your Most Serene Majesty was this: Why does God, since he is just and the avenger of evils, permit such great acts of witchcraft to be done for the destruction of the human race, by which not only sinners, but also many innocent people perish after being gravely tormented?

Why God Permits So Many Evils and Acts of Witchcraft

I remember that, when I was once placed before your Majesty, I answered this question in the following way. The best God, just and upright, gracious and merciful, permits justly whatever he permits, because he is just and there is no iniquity in him; rather, all things that occur, he either does or permits by true judgment. Therefore, when it is asked why God permits evils to be done, we answer: he permits them because he is just. Does the answer we have given seem absurd to your Majesty, O Caesar? For it in no way prejudices the divine goodness that he permits evils to be done by the most just reasoning; indeed it would prejudice it instead if he did not permit evils to be done in the present world. For if he did not permit evils to be done, then man could not sin; he would certainly be incapable of sin, which does not befit his nature, to which the Creator of all things gave free will from the beginning. For since man is a creature and not the Creator, he is necessarily capable of being turned to good as well as to evil, since his existence depends on the supreme Maker of creatures, of all things, just as every caused thing depends upon the cause of its being. But to create has been reserved to God alone, who is incorruptible and everlasting; every corruptible thing necessarily fails, yet it is preserved by the goodness of the creator so long as it does not lose the influence of its cause. Hence it neither could nor ought to have happened that man, by the condition of his own nature, should be created incapable of sinning. That belongs naturally to God alone, the maker of all things, who is unchangeable and everlasting. But whenever it is granted to a human being that he seems unable to sin, the freedom of choice is not taken away, nor is the possibility simply removed; rather, the will is confirmed in the good. And whenever this gift is conferred upon a creature, it is a gift of grace, not of nature. For Scripture says: God created man from the beginning, and left him in the hand of his own counsel. For, properly speaking, it cannot be that mortal man, conceived in original displeasure, should both have free choice and be unable to commit sin. For the most holy bishop Augustine says: The first freedom of the will was to be able not to sin; the last, in glory, will be much greater: not to be able to sin. Therefore, if man could not sin, he would not have dominion over his own will. Hence, although almighty God does not will sin, nevertheless he justly permits human beings to sin and to do evil, so that, while freedom of choice remains, both the virtue of a good work may receive its merit and voluntary depravity may receive the evil it has done. For no one either does good or sins unwillingly. Therefore almighty God justly permits human beings to sin and to do evil, since he granted them freedom of choice from the beginning. Now there are many reasons, long ago assigned by the holy Doctors, why the Almighty permits such great acts of sorcery to be done through the cooperation of demons; of these we shall necessarily make brief mention in order.

The first is so that the excellence of the divine majesty may be made manifest, for he alone is unchangeable and far above every condition. But every mutable creature has no comparison with the unchangeable creator. Hence it is read in Numbers: God is not like a man, that he should lie, nor like a son of man, that he should change. In Isaiah also it is said: God is faithful, without iniquity, just and upright. It is also written in the book of Tobias: You are just, Lord, and all your judgments are true, and all your ways are mercy, truth, and judgment. And in the book of holy Job we read: Far be impiety from God, and iniquity from the Almighty. For he will render to a man his work, and will repay each according to his ways. Therefore every man who rightly understands his own ignorance and weakness plainly recognizes how he stands in comparison with his creator. For God justly permits man to sin, so that freedom of choice may be continued and the excellence of the great God may become known to human beings.

The second reason is so that the unsearchable wisdom of God may become known to mortals, since it knows how to draw good from our evils, when it makes one person’s sin become another’s merit for the increase of virtue. For if evil were not permitted to happen, which of us would understand the good? For God makes and ordains the good; but evils he does not make. Rather, when they have been done by the wicked, he himself disposes them so that they do not come about in a disorderly way. The malice of human beings does not hinder the will of God, nor can a person do anything that God does not permit.

The third cause is that the Almighty permits acts of sorcery to be done in order to manifest his most merciful goodness toward those who have sinned and done penance; he could not show this in any way if he did not permit the creature to sin. For if there were no sinner, God could not be merciful. But because in many things we all offend, everywhere God finds something to forgive; everywhere God meets something in which, as a loving creator, he may show his mercy. Hence the holy bishop Augustine says: If the disease were slight, the physician would be despised and not sought; the disease would not be brought to an end. Therefore, where sin abounded, grace also abounded, by which alone he distinguishes the redeemed from the lost, whom he gathers together into one.

...the mass of perdition, drawn from the origin of creation, preserves as one. Therefore the mercy of the Lord is over all his works.

The fourth reason for divine permission is that the Creator’s justice may be declared against those who have sinned and have not done penance; for if all did good and no one sinned, God’s justice would have nothing to punish. Therefore, so that justice may have a place, the creature sins by divine permission. For the Lord is just, and he will render to each according to the works of his own will.

The fifth reason is the dignity of the human condition: for if God did not permit man to sin, he would seem worse off than the brute beasts, which, with no violence driving them, freely use the motions of nature. For although brute beasts lack reason, nevertheless they have a free motion of nature which they follow; by comparison with them man would seem of a lower condition if he did not have free choice of will. But God permitted man a free will, over which neither kings nor princes rule.

The sixth reason is the praise of the merit of constancy in human virtue, when we praise a just man for this reason: because, although he could have transgressed, he did not transgress, but, with the grace of God helping him, remained in the good constancy of his will.

The seventh reason why almighty God permits demons to do such great works of harmful magic through the agency of witches is this: that those who, having despised truth, take delight in falsehood may be seduced by the devil, the inventor of falsehood, and be utterly deceived. For it is fitting that enchanters and witches, who disdain to follow the saving teachings of Christ, should all be deceived by demons and plunged down to hell, there to be punished forever. They seek aid from demons, the enemies of the whole human race, and they despise the Savior of the world, whom alone they ought to have adored. For it is just that one who, abandoning truth by his own will, clings to falsehood should be hurled by the devil into destruction.

The eighth cause is the manifestation of divine power, whose power and strength is over every creature. Indeed, when almighty God sometimes permits great things to the devil and denies certain small things, he makes manifest in all things how weak the enemy of the human race is, and how subject to the divine majesty. For the devil can do nothing by himself; rather, all the things he does, he does with God permitting them. Therefore the first cause of all, on account of which almighty God permits works of harmful magic to be done, is justice, by which he preserves, in inviolable order, the liberty which he once bestowed upon the creature from the beginning. But because the power of every creature dependent on its Creator is restrained and limited, it is clear that neither the devil can do everything he wishes, nor a man, however depraved in will. The will indeed is free, but power is limited by fixed and necessary degrees. For indeed, if demons could do everything they wished, nothing among human affairs would remain safe, but they would overthrow everything. The story of holy Job shows by a manifest example that the power of demons is bound: Satan did not dare to tempt him any further than had been permitted to him by divine dispensation. For no one in the present world, however just or strong, could resist the fury of demons if, at their own discretion, they could always use a free power to harm. Before the Lord’s Passion, however, they used greater freedom of power than afterward; but when Christ tasted death for us on the altar of the cross, from then on their power was greatly changed, as the Savior says in the Gospel: “Now the prince of the world will be cast out.” For the humility of Christ and the perseverance of the saints greatly restricted the boldness of demons, so that they can rightly be called instigators of evils, but by no means drivers. Nor would the devil gain strength against us unless he received his strength from our sins. Hence Scripture admonishes us, saying: “Resist the devil and he will flee from you.” And again: “Do not give place to the devil.” Therefore, bringing this discourse to a conclusion for the understanding of the proposed question, why God permits so many evil works to be done...

I believe the reasons why he permits harmful acts of magic have been made sufficiently clear. For even if the will of demons is always wicked, their power can never be unjust, since what it wickedly wills it has from its own free choice, but what it is able wickedly to do it has only from God. And these things have been said with regard to those who do evil.

But why does almighty God permit demons, through the agency of witches, to harm people who have been baptized in the name of the holy Trinity and faithfully believe in his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ? For if they could harm only the wicked, the perverse, and unbelievers in body and goods, but were restrained from approaching and injuring the good and faithful, the permission would rightly seem to be a just judgment. But now the good and innocent are more often made sick by the harmful magic of demons, and sometimes are even deprived of life, to pass over in silence the loss of temporal goods which those bewitched often suffer. Thus it comes as a scruple to many why the Almighty permits these things, since he permits nothing unjustly.

For this proposed question I shall set out in order, as briefly as I can, the necessary reasons, no others than those I have received from ancient and Catholic doctors. The first reason is the testing of Christians’ faith and the proving of their integrity, so that, when scourged by the harmful works of demons, they may learn in the sufferings of the flesh what faith and love toward God they have hidden in the mind. It is not difficult to be patient in prosperity; but in adversity, with humble patience, to await help from the Savior of the faithful belongs not to the soft, but to the strong and truly faithful Christians. In his tribulation most holy Job learned how great a constancy of faith toward God he had, he who previously in tranquility had preserved piety without the dart of temptation. Here it must also be noted that those whom harmful acts of demons or of men have in any way made sick, and who, to recover health, either approach or consult any sorcerers and enchanters, whether by themselves or through others, act against the commandments of God and of the Church, and have neither true faith in God nor love. For they prefer the health of mortal flesh to God, and seek salvation not from Christ, but from the devil and his minister. They prefer to live healthy, but unhappily, in the name of the devil, rather than suffer a little here for the love of Christ and afterward rejoice with him forever. But one who does not approach sorcerers because God has forbidden it, preferring to live with observance of God’s commandments in poverty and sickness rather than against God in riches and bodily health, truly loves God and rightly preserves the integrity of the Christian faith. Among Christians, O most sacred Caesar, men corrupt in mind and reprobate concerning the faith must not be tolerated: those who cure the bewitched by harmful magic, who reveal thefts and adulteries by the ministry of demons, who foretell future things by inspection of stones or mirrors. Do not listen, I pray, to those who, ignorant of the divine laws, think ministers of demons of this kind useful to your rule because one skilled in harmful magic knows how to undo harmful magic; for this pernicious healing of bodies brings death to souls, and makes human beings withdraw from God, the creator of all things, and cling to impious apostate demons, with whom after death they will be damned forever.

The second reason why almighty God permits the innocent to be harmed by harmful magic is the increase of merits, so that, once their patience has been tested in tribulation, they may deserve a more worthy crown of glory in heaven. For, as holy Augustine says, a person is unknown to himself as to what he can bear and what he cannot bear. At times he fears that he cannot bear what nevertheless he can. When temptation approaches like a certain interrogator, a person is discovered by himself, who before, hidden, did not know himself. The divine chief apostle Peter, before temptation came upon him, was hidden both from himself and from others as to how inconsiderate and weak he was; that temptation approached, and it became apparent The weakness that had lain hidden appeared. Therefore temptation is the greatest test of a person, as sacred Scripture bears witness: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people.” Patience is easy in prosperity, because no adversities strike the mind. But the tribulations of the righteous are many, and from all of them our Lord Jesus Christ will deliver them.

The third reason for divine permission is the guarding of humility, so that a faithful and righteous person may always fear God and never rely on his own strength or righteousness. Hence Scripture says of the reprobate: “They are not in the labor of men, and they will not be scourged with men; therefore pride has held them fast. They are covered with their iniquity and impiety; their iniquity has come forth, as it were, from fatness.” It is the mercy of God that he sometimes permits good and righteous people to be shaken by adversities, when he knows that they cannot be humbled in prosperity. For tribulation has made many humble whom favorable circumstances would have made proud. Finally, the fearful imagining of acts of sorcery makes a good person fear his God and diligently call upon his help; fortified by that help, he can trust that he is safe against the assaults of demons. But no proud person, presuming on his own powers, should think himself safe from the sorceries of demons, because the person whom God’s protection abandons when he is swollen with pride undoubtedly lies open to the sorceries of demons.

The fourth reason is that there may be a distinction between the good and the evil. For Scripture says in the Acts of the Apostles concerning good people beloved by God: “Through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God.” And holy Paul, lover of Christ, says in a certain epistle: “All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution.” Likewise the most wise King Solomon says in Proverbs: “The Lord corrects the one whom he loves, and, like a father, takes pleasure in his son.” It is a most glorious thing for a Christian to endure adversities patiently for the love of God, whether they are brought upon him by wicked people or by demons. For power is given to the devil and his ministers to harm good and righteous people, not for their confusion, as the Petrones suppose, but rather for the very great and certain consolation of the soul. Indeed, when a righteous person lives well, harms no one, offends no one, does injury to no one, loves, fears, and venerates his God with his whole heart, keeps his commandments with all diligence, and nevertheless is afflicted by sorcerers, whether in body, in possessions, or in both, that person is truly blessed: for when he has been tested he will receive the crown of life that God has promised to those who love him. Everyone who lives rightly in the unity of the faith of the Catholic Church of Christians, and, receiving evils in this world, patiently endures them for the love of God, has a sure sign that he perseveres in the grace of God and will be saved. Therefore we read this written concerning the wicked and reprobate: “Why do the impious live? They have been lifted up and strengthened with riches. Their houses are secure and peaceful, and the rod of God is not upon them. They spend their days amid good things, and in a moment they descend to hell.”

For it is a manifest sign of damnation if a person lives here badly in sins and vices, contrary to God, and is prospered in the goods of fortune and in bodily health.

The fifth reason why the Almighty permits good and righteous people to be afflicted by the wicked and reprobate is for the complete purification of the mind. For, as Scripture says: “There is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin.” But since God lets no sin pass unpunished, in his mercy he has ordained temporal penalties for righteous people for their offenses, but eternal penalties in his justice for the impious and reprobate. Therefore in his mercy he changes the eternal penalty for the penitent into a temporal one, which they must necessarily suffer either in this world or after death in purgatory. But because the torments of purgatory are dreadful and very severe, merciful God is accustomed to purge in this life, in various ways, the penitents whom he loves, through the inconveniences of different tribulations in body and possessions. For acts of sorcery are beneficial to the impious ...of wicked men are a remedy for good and just people, but for those who inflict them they lead to damnation.

The sixth reason is that a person harmed by the assaults of demons may be called back to repentance and may resolve in his heart upon the necessary amendment of life. For almighty God does not immediately send vengeance when we sin, but awaits our amendment until the appointed time. But if we have neglected to do penance, the avenger of evils comes to us when we do not expect it; and we who, as sinners, disdained to acknowledge him by repenting in tranquillity, will at last, though late, acknowledge him in tribulation. Hence the holy prophet speaks in the person of God, saying: “If his sons forsake my law, and do not walk in my judgments, and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges; but my mercy I will not scatter from them, nor will I do harm in my truth.”

The seventh reason why almighty God permits the sorceries of demons to prevail against the good and innocent is so that an excessively licentious occasion for sinning may be cut off from them. For there are many poor and infirm people pleasing to God, good, devout, and humble, whom want and bodily sickness preserve in the love of God. If they were rich and raised up with honors, they would quickly flow down from their purpose of holiness into the depth of vices. It is not expedient for everyone’s salvation to have honors and riches together with health; nor does a longer life always make a person better. Therefore almighty God, wishing to show his mercy toward those whom he has chosen, permits the good, the just, and the innocent to be subject to various calamities; and sometimes through demons, sometimes through evil people, sometimes by various other ways and means, he takes away from such people riches and honors, which he foreknew they would use badly, so that they may preserve humility in poverty and low estate, which, if placed in wealth and high rank, they would by no means have preserved. He also quite often permits many great illnesses to befall them, because cheerful bodily health would have brought upon them the greatest sickness of mind. Finally, he permits certain people to be driven to death by sorcery, so that the license for sinning may be cut off from them, which they would have abused if allowed to live longer. Hence Scripture says of the just man: “He was snatched away lest wickedness alter his understanding, and lest deceit beguile his soul.”

The eighth reason for divine permission is that people may venerate the sacraments of the Church, which have great power against all the sorceries of malignant spirits. For a person is rarely harmed by the sorceries of demons if he venerates the sacraments and rites of the Catholic Church with due honor. And we have very often heard, from the witches’ own confession, that hearing Masses and using things blessed by the Church greatly weakens the powers of demons. For they are not blessed in the Church of God in vain, but so that they may be fearsome signs which show demons the protection of divine protection.

Concerning boys and infants, however, who, having been reborn in Christ, are sometimes killed by the sorceries of demons or of human beings, we do not doubt that divine providence permits this to happen for their salvation, for it knows how to order all things for the better for mortals. Yet it often happens that infants perish by sorceries because of the sins of their parents.

A Celebrated Medicinal Powder of Trithemius

Many have always praised this powder of Trithemius, very useful for the brain for students, down to the present. For quite a few, by using it, have reached the point that they could easily disregard those examiners of urine, arteries, tongues, and excrement. Many have prolonged robust age almost to the hundredth year; finally, they have attained such sharpness of memory that they easily surpassed anyone, even the greatest. And this without pills, clysters, poultices, ointments, plasters, electuaries, chewing preparations, gargles, little bags, fumes, preserves, syrups, waters, theriacs, and the like.

Recipe: Calamus aromaticus, Gentian, Cumin, Mountain siler, Anise, Medicinal Powder

Of anise, caraway, ammi, parsley seed, spikenard, of each ʒ s.

Of red coral; of pearls, or unpierced pearls, ʒ v.

Of white ginger, bitter-sweet (Chamepyt), leaves of hay; of burnt tartar, of each ʒ v.

Of mace, cubebs, of each ʒ ij.

Of cloves, ʒ vij.

Let a powder be made according to art.

Its dose is ʒ s., to be taken morning and evening, in broth or wine, for the first month. In the second month, only in the morning; in the third month, in the morning three times a week; and so thereafter it is to be continued for life. For it is effective against many illnesses and is a most tested Medicinal. 127

and efficacious powder. It strengthens the stomach, purges the brain, clears the eyes and sight, sharpens the memory, consumes bad and superfluous humors throughout the whole body without danger, soothes and opens constriction in the chest, drives away nausea, prevents excessive fatness, preserves from epilepsy and apoplexy, dissolves the material of stone without pain, and does not permit it to harden into a stone; it does not allow chiragra, podagra, or sciatica to prevail. When Paulus Scalichius wished to give this powder for use to the Duke of Prussia, whose councillor he was at that time, the prince’s physicians forbade it; from this there arose a dispute among them, in which the case for and against that powder was fought out in writings. That dispute is extant in Scalichius’s own Philosophical Satires.
